description: We are a team passionate about space exploration, physics, and engineering. For Flame in Freefall, we aim to explore how fire behaves in microgravity and use NASA research and data to better understand fire safety for astronauts. We hope to combine scientific research, coding, and creative problem-solving to develop an informative, interactive tool that helps make space missions safer.
summary:
Flame Intelligence (Team Blue Frogs)

Fire behaves very differently in space. Without gravity, flames form spheres, can burn almost invisibly at lower temperatures, and give off smoke that standard detectors can miss. On a spacecraft, astronauts have nowhere to escape. Flame Intelligence turns decades of NASA microgravity fire research into one searchable tool for Moon and Mars missions.

We collected more than 170 sources from NASA’s Technical Reports Server, open experiment datasets and mission reports, and graded each one by how strong its evidence is. Users can search and filter experiments, compare results across fuels and gravity levels, and view a ranked list of the biggest fire risks for lunar and Martian habitats. An AI research assistant answers questions using only this NASA evidence and cites every source. It also keeps confirmed findings separate from its own interpretation and flags any limits in the data.

The goal is to help engineers and mission planners understand fire risks before they build, so habitats are safer before the first fire.
details:
Flame Intelligence is a website that turns decades of NASA microgravity fire research into one searchable tool. We collected 171 records from NASA’s Technical Reports Server, open experiment datasets and mission reports, then tagged each one by fuel, gravity level and experiment and graded how strong its evidence is. Users can search and compare experiments, see patterns on a dashboard, and view a ranked list of the biggest fire risks for Moon and Mars habitats. An AI research assistant answers questions using only this NASA evidence. It cites every source and keeps confirmed findings separate from its own interpretation.

NASA’s fire research is spread across hundreds of hard-to-search reports, so our site saves engineers, students and mission planners hours of work. Our goal is to help designers understand fire risks before they build, so habitats are safer before the first fire.

We built the site with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, used a Python build script, and hosted it on Netlify, where server functions written in Node.js keep our API keys hidden. Google Gemini powers the AI, Groq is an automatic backup, and we used Claude to help with coding and design.

What makes it creative is that the AI can’t make things up. It is limited to NASA evidence and flags anything unverified. Our team focused on accuracy, reliability, security, ease of use, and being honest about where NASA’s data has gaps.
